ABSTRACT            
Skeletal muscle absorbs long chain fatty acids (LCFA) that are either oxidized in 
mitochondria or temporarily stored as triglycerides in lipid droplets (LDs). So far, it is still 
not fully understood how muscle lipid uptake and storage is regulated and whether it is 
important for whole-body lipid homeostasis. Here we show that the small GTPase Rab8a 
regulates muscle lipid uptake and storage in skeletal muscle. Muscle-specific Rab8a deletion 
caused hyperlipidemia and exacerbated high fat diet (HFD)-induced hepatosteatosis. 
Mechanistically, Rab8a deficiency decreased LCFA entry into skeletal muscle, and also 
inhibited LD fusion in muscle cells. Consequently, blood lipid levels were elevated and 
caused stimulation of hepatic mTOR, which enhanced hepatosteatosis through upregulation 
of hepatic lipogenesis and cholesterol biosynthesis. Our results demonstrate the significance 
of muscle lipid uptake and storage in regulating whole-body lipid homeostasis, and shed light 
on roles of skeletal muscle in the pathogenesis of hyperlipidemia and hepatosteatosis.

INTRODUCTION 
Metabolic diseases including obesity, type 2 diabetes, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease 
(NAFLD) have become prevalent worldwide in recent years, which urges a better 
understanding of their pathogenesis for improvement in the prevention and treatment. 
Skeletal muscle, as the largest organ in our body, has a critical role in regulating whole-body 
metabolic homeostasis (1), though its roles in the pathogenesis of metabolic diseases are still 
not fully understood. 
 After a meal, nutrients including glucose and lipids surge into the blood. Up to 70% 
of post-prandial glucose is absorbed by skeletal muscle and stored as glycogen, which is a 
critical process for maintaining blood glucose levels (1). Entry of glucose into skeletal 
muscle is mainly mediated by the glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4) that can translocate from its 
intracellular storage sites onto the plasma membrane in response to insulin (2). Insulin also 
stimulates translocation of a fatty acid translocase CD36 onto the plasma membrane to 
mediate uptake of long chain fatty acids (LCFA) in skeletal muscle (3; 4). Once absorbed, 
LCFA can be channeled into the mitochondria for oxidation (5) or esterified to form 
triglycerides for storage in lipid droplets (LDs) (6). LDs are cytoplasmic organelles that have 
a phospholipid monolayer coat surrounding a neutral lipid core composed of triglycerides 
and/or cholesterol esters (7). Although skeletal muscle is not classically considered as an 
important lipid storage organ, its lipid stores can still make up ~8% of total body lipids (8). 
Under HFD conditions, skeletal muscle can accumulate more neutral lipids with enlarged 
LDs (9; 10).

Rab8a is a small GTPase that plays crucial roles in membrane trafficking, and it 
might be involved in the regulation of both lipid and glucose metabolism. Rab8a-deficiency 
inhibits nutrient absorption in the small intestine and causes premature death in mice due to 
mislocalization of apical proteins such as peptidases and transporters to the lysosome for 
degradation in intestinal epithelial cells (11). Rab8a has been implicated in regulating 
insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation in L6 muscle cells (12; 13) and CD36 translocation 
in HL-1 cardiomyocytes (14). Down-regulation of Rab8a via small-interfering RNA (siRNA) 
inhibits insulin-stimulated translocation of GLUT4 or CD36 in these culture cells (12-14). 
LDs can grow in size through either fusion of two smaller LDs into one larger LD (15) or 
addition of neutral lipids into pre-existing droplets (16). It has also been shown that Rab8a 
regulates LD fusion in 3T3-L1 adipocytes (17). Given the importance of LDs and 
insulin-stimulated translocation of GLUT4 and CD36 in skeletal muscle, we hypothesize that 
Rab8a may have a critical metabolic role in skeletal muscle, which may influence 
whole-body metabolic homeostasis.    
In this study, we took a genetic approach to investigate impacts of Rab8a-deficiency 
in skeletal muscle on metabolic homeostasis in this tissue as well as at the whole-body level. 
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS 
Materials 
Recombinant human insulin was purchased from Novo Nordisk (Denmark). 
Rapamycin (S1039) and fenofibrate (S1794) were from Selleck Chemicals (USA). Bodipy 
493/503 (D-3922) and Bodipy 558/568 C12 (D-3835) were from Thermo Fisher Scientific 
(USA). 2-deoxy-D-[1,2-3H(N)]glucose, D-[1-14C]-mannitol and [14C(U)]-palmitic acid were

from PerkinElmer (USA). All other chemicals were from Sigma-Aldrich or Sangon Biotech 
(Shanghai, China). The antibodies are listed in Supplementary Table 1. 
Mouse breeding and husbandry  
The Ethics Committee at Nanjing University approved all animal studies. The 
Rab8af/f mice were as previously described (11) and back-crossed with C57BL6 mice for at 
least 8 generations before experiments. The Myf5-Cre mice were as previously described 
(18). Mice were housed with a light/dark cycle of 12 h, and free access to food and water 
unless stated. 
Blood chemistry 
Blood glucose levels were determined using a Breeze-2 glucometer (Bayer). Serum 
free fatty acid (FFA), triglyceride (TG) and total cholesterol (TC) were measured as 
previously described (19). 
Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) and insulin tolerance test (ITT) 
Mice were deprived of food overnight (16 h for the OGTT) or for 4 h (for the ITT). 
For the OGTT, a bolus of glucose (1.5 mg/g) was administered into mice via oral gavage. For 
the ITT, 0.75 mU/g of insulin was intraperitoneally injected into mice. Blood glucose levels 
were determined through tail bleeding. 
Body composition analysis 
Body composition was measured on isoflurane-anaesthetized mice via dual-energy 
X-ray absorptiometry using a Lunar PIXImus-II densitometer (GE Healthcare). Images taken 
with the PIXImus-II densitometer were analyzed using PIXImus-II software. 
Measurement of liver TG and TC

Liver TG was measured as previously described (19). For liver TC, lipids were 
extracted with chloroform:isopropanol:NP-40 (7:11:0.1), and TC was measured after removal 
of organic solvent using LabAssay Cholesterol kit (294-65801) (Wako Chemicals USA).  
Cell culture and transfection 
Rat L6 myoblasts were obtained from Cell Resource Center, Chinese Academy of 
Medical Sciences (China) and maintained in medium containing 10% (v/v) foetal bovine 
serum. Lipofectamine-mediated transfection of L6 myoblasts was carried out as previously 
described (20). Rab8a siRNA used for knockdown experiments is as previously described 
(17). 
Measurement of LD sizes and neutral lipid exchange rate  
Sizes of largest LDs and lipid exchange rates in L6 myoblasts were measured as 
previously described (17). 
Muscle incubation and glucose uptake ex vivo 
Soleus or EDL muscles were isolated and subjected to stimulation with or without 
insulin, and muscle glucose uptake was carried out as previously described (21). 
Muscle lipid uptake and oxidation ex vivo 
Muscle lipid uptake and oxidation was measured as previously described with 
modifications (22). Briefly, isolated soleus muscles were stimulated with or without insulin 
for 30 min, and then incubated in KRB buffer (+/- insulin) containing 14C-palmitic acid for 
50 min. At the completion of incubation, muscles were blotted dry and lysed for 
measurements of radioisotopes within them using a Tri-Carb 2800TR scintillation counter. 
Gaseous 14CO2 was evolved from incubation media with 0.6 M perchloric acid and trapped in

benzethonium hydroxide soaked filters. Radioactivity in trapped 14CO2 was measured and 
used to determine muscle lipid oxidation. The sum of radioactivity in muscle and gaseous 
14CO2 was used to calculate muscle lipid uptake rates. 
Biotinylation of membrane proteins 
Biotinylation of cell surface proteins was performed as previously described with 
modifications (23). Briefly, isolated soleus muscles were stimulated with or without insulin 
for 50 min, and then incubated in KRB buffer (+/- insulin) containing Sulfo-NHS-SS-Biotin 
(Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30 min. Biotinylated surface proteins were precipitated from 
lysates using NeutrAvidin-Agarose (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and surface levels of GLUT4 
and CD36 were determined via western blotting using the respective antibodies.  
Tissue lysis, subcellular fractionation of the BAT, and immunoblotting 
Mouse tissues were harvested, homogenized and analyzed via immunoblotting as 
previously described (21). Subcellular fractionation was performed in the BAT as previously 
described (21). 
Real-time Quantitative PCR 
Real-time Quantitative PCR was performed using an Applied Biosystems® 
StepOnePlusTM system and the primers listed in Supplementary Table 2 to measure 
expression levels of target genes. 
Immunofluorescence staining and imaging 
Immunofluorescence staining was performed as previously described (20). Briefly, 
frozen sections of tissues or paraformaldehyde-fixed single muscle fibers were sequentially 
incubated with primary antibodies and Alexa Fluor®-conjugated or Cy3/Cy5-conjugated

mounted and photographed with a Leica or Olympus confocal microscope. 
Statistical analysis 
Data are given as the mean ± SD. Comparisons were carried out via t-test for two 
groups or via 2-way ANOVA for multiple groups using Prism software (GraphPad, San 
Diego, CA, USA). 
RESULTS 
Deletion of Rab8a in the Myf5-lineage caused hyperlipidemia and exacerbated obesity 
and hepatic steatosis in HFD-fed mice 
Skeletal muscle cells originates from Myf5-lineage progenitors. We mated the 
Rab8af/f mouse (11) with the Myf5-Cre mouse (18) to delete Rab8a in Myf5-lineage-derived 
tissues including skeletal muscle in the resultant Rab8af/f/Myf5-Cre mice (named as 
Rab8a-mKO) (Supple. Fig. 1). As expected, Rab8a expression was diminished in 
Myf5-lineage-derived tissues including skeletal muscle and brown adipose tissue (BAT) of 
Rab8a-mKO mice but not in other tissues analyzed (Fig. 1A). No apparent compensation was 
observed for expression of the related Rab8b, Rab10 and Rab13 in skeletal muscle of 
Rab8a-mKO mice (Supple. Fig. 2A-C). When mice were fed on chow diet, neither body 
weight nor composition were distinguishable between the Rab8a-mKO and Rab8af/f mice 
(Fig. 1B-C, Supple. Fig. 3A-C). No difference was observed for blood glucose between the 
two genotypes under either ad libitum fed or overnight fasted conditions (Fig. 1E, Supple. 
Fig. 4). Plasma FFA, TG and TC were also unaltered in the Rab8a-mKO mice under ad

Diabetes

9
libitum fed conditions (Supple. Fig. 4). However, plasma FFA and TG levels were 
significantly higher in the Rab8a-mKO mice than in the Rab8af/f controls after an overnight 
fast (Fig. 1E). When fed on high fat diet (HFD), the Rab8a-mKO mice were heavier and 
contained more fat than the controls, but they had normal lean mass (Fig. 1B and D, Supple. 
Fig. 3D-E). Similar to when on chow diet, the Rab8a-mKO mice had normal blood glucose 
but higher levels of plasma FFA, TG and TC than the controls on HFD after an overnight fast 
(Fig. 1F). Besides the hyperlipidemia and obese phenotype, the Rab8a-mKO mice had 
heavier livers and developed hepatosteatosis (Fig. 1G-I). Their livers had larger LDs (Supple. 
Fig. 5A-B) and contained more TG and TC than the controls (Fig. 1H-I).  
Insulin-stimulated glucose uptake was normal in Rab8a-deficient skeletal muscle 
Since Rab8a has been implicated in regulating GLUT4 trafficking in L6 muscle cells 
(12), we investigated whether its deletion in skeletal muscle could inhibit insulin-stimulated 
glucose uptake, which might indirectly affect lipid metabolism. We found that the insulin 
signaling pathway remained intact in Rab8a-deficient skeletal muscle as evidenced by normal 
phosphorylation of PKB, AS160 and GSK3 (Fig. 2A-B, Supple. Fig. 6A-B). GLUT4 protein 
expression was also normal in Rab8a-deficient muscle (Fig. 2C-D). We then examined 
insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation in soleus muscle and found no difference between 
the two genotypes (Fig. 2C and E, Supple. Fig. 6C). In agreement with the unaltered GLUT4 
translocation, insulin-stimulated glucose uptake remained intact in both soleus and EDL 
muscle from the Rab8a-mKO mice (Fig. 2F-G). Furthermore, the Rab8a-mKO mice 
displayed normal glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity (Supple. Fig. 6D and F), and their 
insulin secretion remained normal upon glucose challenge (Supple. Fig. 6E). These data

show that Rab8a does not play an important role in regulating insulin-stimulated glucose 
uptake in skeletal muscle, and the hyperlipidemia and hepatosteatosis of the Rab8a-mKO 
mice was not due to an alteration in muscle glucose uptake. 
Muscle LCFA uptake was decreased due to impaired CD36 translocation and 
expression in the Rab8a-mKO mice 
Discovery of the hyperlipidemia phenotype promoted us to investigate whether 
muscle lipid metabolism was impaired in the Rab8a-mKO mice. As expected, LCFA uptake 
was increased by more than 2-fold in wild-type soleus muscle in response to insulin (Fig. 3A). 
In contrast, insulin could no longer stimulate LCFA uptake in Rab8a-deficient muscle (Fig. 
3A). As a consequence, fatty acid oxidation was elevated by more than 2-fold in response to 
insulin in wild-type soleus muscle, however this insulin response was blunted in 
Rab8a-deficient muscle (Fig. 3B). In agreement with their defective muscle LCFA uptake, 
the Rab8a-mKO mice were unable to efficiently clear lipids in the blood after an oral lipid 
load as compared with the Rab8af/f littermates (Fig. 3C-D). It was possible that hepatic output 
of TG through secretion of TG-rich very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) might also 
contribute to hyperlipidemia in the Rab8a-mKO mice. To address this possibility, we treated 
mice with an inhibitor tyloxapol targeting lipoprotein lipase (LPL) that is a key enzyme to 
hydrolyze TG in VLDL to release FFA for absorption by skeletal muscle. Tyloxapol 
significantly elevated blood TG in the Rab8af/f mice but failed to exert such an effect in the 
Rab8a-mKO mice within 2 h after administration (Fig. 3E). These data demonstrated that 
impaired muscle lipid uptake but not hepatic VLDL secretion most likely underlay the 
hyperlipidemia phenotype in the Rab8a-mKO mice.

Muscle lipid uptake has been reported to be mainly mediated by CD36, which 
undergoes translocation in response to insulin in skeletal muscle (3). We found that Rab8a 
partially colocalized with CD36 in skeletal muscle (Fig. 3F). When Rab8a was 
knocked-down in L6 myotubes, it did not affect expression of CD36 but impaired 
insulin-stimulated CD36 translocation (Fig. 3G). Consistently, insulin increased CD36 levels 
at the cell surface by more than 2-fold in wild-type skeletal muscle. However, 
insulin-stimulated CD36 translocation was significantly inhibited in Rab8a-deficient muscle 
despite its normal expression in these young Rab8a-mKO mice (3-month-old) (Fig. 3H-J). 
Interestingly, muscle CD36 protein levels were markedly decreased in older Rab8a-mKO 
mice (6-month-old) as compared with their Rab8af/f littermate controls despite normal mRNA 
levels in skeletal muscle from these mice on a chow diet (Fig. 4A-B). When mice were 
transferred from chow to a HFD, CD36 mRNA levels increased in the Rab8af/f muscle but 
remained largely unchanged in the Rab8a-deficient muscle (Fig. 4B). Moreover, CD36 
protein levels were still lower in skeletal muscle from the Rab8a-mKO mice on HFD (Fig. 
4C-D). In contrast to CD36, two other membrane proteins, namely GLUT4 and transferrin 
receptor (TfR), were not altered in Rab8a-deficient skeletal muscle (Fig. 4C). Interestingly, 
we found that LPL expression was significantly decreased in Rab8a-deficient skeletal muscle 
at both mRNA and protein levels (Fig. 4B-C). Diminution of LPL suggested that degradation 
of TG from VLDL might be impaired. In agreement, more TG was detected in the VLDL 
fractions from the Rab8a-mKO mice (Supple. Fig. 7). LPL is a target gene of PPARα (24; 
25), whose expression was normal in skeletal muscle of Rab8a-mKO mice (Fig. 4B-C). Fatty 
acids are ligands for PPARα, and CD36 is a known regulator of PPARα through ligand

activation (26). It is therefore likely that decreased uptake of lipids into skeletal muscle due 
to impaired CD36 translocation/expression might lower PPARα activity, which might 
consequently decrease LPL expression in Rab8a-deficient skeletal muscle. 
Rab8a was also deleted in the BAT of Rab8a-mKO mice, however its deletion did not 
affect expression of total or cell surface CD36 in this tissue (Supple. Fig. 8). Expression of 
key genes involved in lipid transport, lipogenesis, lipolysis and β-oxidation were normal, but 
thermogenic genes were increased in the BAT of Rab8a-mKO mice (Supple. Fig. 8B-D), 
suggesting that thermogenic function of the BAT might not be impaired in these mice. 
Furthermore, specific deletion of Rab8a in the BAT and white adipose tissue via an 
AdipoQ-Cre did not cause hyperlipidemia and hepatosteatosis (Supple. Fig. 9). These data 
suggest that Rab8a-deficiency in the BAT was most likely not responsible for the 
hyperlipidemia and hepatosteatosis phenotype in the Rab8a-mKO mice although we cannot 
rule out the possibility that Rab8a deletion in the WAT might counteract possible effects 
from the BAT in the Rab8a adipose-specific knockout mice. 
Together, these data show that entry of lipids into skeletal muscle was impaired in the 
Rab8a-mKO mice probably due to inhibition of CD36 translocation and down-regulation of 
CD36 expression, which may explain the hyperlipidemia in these mice. 
LD fusion was impaired in Rab8a-deficient muscle cells 
A portion of lipids absorbed into skeletal muscle is temporally stored in LDs. When 
mice were fed on HFD, LDs became enlarged in skeletal muscle from the Rab8af/f controls. 
Although LDs in Rab8a-deficient skeletal muscle still became enlarged, they were 
substantially smaller than those in control muscle under HFD conditions (Fig. 5A-B). It has

Diabetes

13
been shown that Rab8a regulates LD fusion in adipocytes (17). Therefore, in addition to 
impaired lipid uptake, defective LD fusion might be another underlying cause of the smaller 
LDs in Rab8a-deficient skeletal muscle. In agreement with this possibility, Rab8a partially 
colocalized with LDs within muscle fibers (Fig. 5A-B) and L6 cells (Supple. Fig. 10A-B). 
We then employed L6 cells to examine a possible role of Rab8a in regulating LD fusion in 
muscle cells. Interestingly, the sizes and lipid exchange rates of LDs were both significantly 
decreased when Rab8a was down-regulated in L6 cells (Fig. 5C-F, Supple. Fig. 10C-D), 
suggesting that Rab8a-deficiency inhibited LD fusion in muscle cells. The Rab8a-mKO mice 
displayed normal expression of adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL, an important lipase for 
lipolysis) at both the mRNA and protein levels, indicating that their skeletal muscle lipolysis 
might be unaltered (Fig. 4B-C). Together, these data demonstrate that Rab8a deficiency 
decreases lipid storage in part through impairing LD fusion in muscle cells. 
Hepatic lipogenesis and cholesterol biosynthesis were enhanced in the Rab8a-mKO 
mice To gain insights into how muscle deficiency of Rab8a exacerbated HFD-induced 
hepatosteatosis, we examined expression of key genes in lipid metabolism in the liver. The 
mRNA levels of lipogenic genes such as Acc1, Fasn and Scd1, and protein levels of FASN 
were up-regulated in the liver of Rab8a-mKO mice on both chow diet and HFD (Fig. 6A and 
D), suggesting that hepatic lipogenesis was elevated in these mice. Moreover, mRNA 
expression of GPAT1, a key enzyme for hepatic triglyceride synthesis, was up-regulated in 
the liver of Rab8a-mKO mice (Fig. 6D). Similarly, cholesterol biosynthesis might also be 
increased in the liver of these mice as evidenced by elevated mRNA levels of cholesterol 
biosynthetic genes such as Hmgcs1, Hmgcr, Fdps, Cyp51a1 and Dhcr7 (Fig. 6E).

Furthermore, expression of LDL-receptor was up-regulated in the liver of Rab8a-mKO mice 
on both chow diet and HFD (Fig. 6A and E). In contrast, hepatic expression of key lipolytic 
enzymes PNPLA3 and ATGL, and key regulators for β-oxidation such as PPARα, ACADL 
and CPT1, were all normal in the liver of Rab8a-mKO mice (Fig. 6A and F). Together, these 
data suggest that exacerbated hepatosteatosis in HFD-fed Rab8a-mKO mice was most likely 
due to enhanced lipogenesis, triglyceride synthesis and cholesterol biosynthesis in the liver of 
these animals. 
In contrast to the liver, no significant alteration in the key genes involved in lipid 
metabolism was detected in the adipose tissue of Rab8a-mKO mice on either chow diet or 
HFD (Supple. Fig. 11A-B). 
Activation of the mTOR pathway enhanced hepatic lipogenesis and cholesterol 
biosynthesis in the Rab8a-mKO mice    
We next sought to find out potential mechanisms for enhanced hepatic lipogenesis 
and cholesterol biosynthesis in the Rab8a-mKO mice. SREBP1 is a common regulator for the 
above-mentioned lipogenic genes (27; 28), whose mRNA and full-length protein levels were 
normal in the liver of Rab8a-mKO mice (Fig. 6A-B). Full-length SREBP1 (flSREBP1) 
resides on the endoplasmic reticulum, where its N-terminal part can be cleaved off and 
thereafter is translocated into the nucleus to regulate transcription of lipogenic genes. 
Importantly, the cleaved nuclear form of SREBP1 (nSREBP1) was increased in the liver of 
Rab8a-mKO mice despite normal expression of flSREBP1 (Fig. 6A). Consistent with the 
cleavage of SREBP1 being under control of mTOR (29; 30), mTOR activation as evidenced 
by its own phosphorylation and phosphorylation of its substrates S6K and 4EBP1 was

increased in the liver of Rab8a-mKO mice on both chow diet and HFD (Fig. 6B). The 
activity of SREBP1 in the nucleus is inhibited by lipin1, whose phosphorylation by mTOR 
prevents its entry into the nucleus (31). Consistent with mTOR activation, phosphorylation of 
lipin1 was elevated in the liver of Rab8a-mKO mice (Fig. 6B), which indicates a higher 
activity of SREBP1 in the nucleus. Activation of mTOR was not due to the upstream 
regulators PKB and TSC2 since their phosphorylation remained normal in the liver of 
Rab8a-mKO mice (Fig. 6C). To establish a causal relationship between mTOR activation and 
upregulation of hepatic lipogenesis and cholesterol biosynthesis, we treated the Rab8a-mKO 
and Rab8af/f mice with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin. Rapamycin decreased 
phosphorylation of mTOR and lipin1, and normalized nSREBP1 levels in the liver of 
Rab8a-mKO mice (Fig. 7A). Consequently, expression of lipogenic and cholesterol 
biosynthetic genes was normalized in the rapamycin-treated liver of Rab8a-mKO mice (Fig. 
7B), which further confirmed that increased expression in lipogenic genes in the liver of 
Rab8a-mKO mice was due to mTOR activation. Importantly, rapamycin treatment 
normalized TC levels in the liver of Rab8a-mKO mice (Fig. 7D). It has been shown that 
lipids can activate mTOR (32; 33), which led us to speculate that hyperlipidemia might 
underlie mTOR activation in the liver of Rab8a-mKO mice. Treatment with a lipid-lowering 
drug fenofibrate significantly decreased serum FFA, TG and TC in these mice (Supple. Fig. 
12). Indeed, fenofibrate treatment attenuated activation of the mTOR-lipin1 pathway and 
lowered hepatic expression of lipogenic and cholesterol biosynthetic genes in the 
Rab8a-mKO mice (Fig. 7E-F). Together, these data show that elevated serum lipid levels

might activate the mTOR-lipin1-SREBP1 pathway that consequently enhance lipogenesis 
and cholesterol biosynthesis in the liver of Rab8a-mKO mice. 
In agreement with unaltered expression of key genes of lipid metabolism in adipose 
(Supple. Fig. 11A), the mTOR-lipin1 pathway remained normal in this tissue of Rab8a-mKO 
mice (Supple. Fig. 11B).  
DISCUSSIONS 
In this study, we show that Rab8a regulates lipid uptake and LD fusion in skeletal 
muscle. Its deficiency in skeletal muscle impairs muscle lipid uptake and storage, and causes 
hyperlipidemia and exacerbates HFD-induced hepatosteatosis through promoting lipogenesis 
and cholesterol biosynthesis in the liver (Fig. 8). Our findings shed light on a new role of 
skeletal muscle in the pathogenesis of hyperlipidemia and NAFLD.    
Rab8a has been implicated in regulating various membrane trafficking processes 
including GLUT4 trafficking (12) and CD36 trafficking (14). The majority of published 
studies were carried out in culture cell lines, and the in vivo functions of Rab8a have only 
been studied in small intestine using the Rab8a knockout mice (11). Despite the importance 
of Rab8a in regulating GLUT4 trafficking in L6 muscle cells (12), our in vivo studies show 
that it was dispensable for glucose uptake in mouse skeletal muscle. It is currently not clear 
whether there are compensatory responses to regulate GLUT4 translocation and glucose 
uptake in the Rab8a-deficient skeletal muscle. In agreement with a role in regulating CD36 
trafficking in HL-1 cardiomyocytes (14), Rab8a was required for insulin-stimulated CD36 
translocation in mouse skeletal muscle. Regulation of CD36 translocation by Rab8a 
displayed a tissue-dependent manner. Its deletion impaired insulin-stimulated CD36

Diabetes

--- Page 17 ---

 
17
translocation in skeletal muscle but not in the BAT. Nevertheless, Rab8a deletion in the BAT 
might contribute to some of the phenotypes observed in the Rab8a-mKO mice through 
yet-unidentified mechanisms. We note that Rab8a was also indispensable for maintaining 
CD36 protein levels in older mice. It has been shown that Rab8a deficiency causes 
mislocalization of apical peptidases and transporters to the lysosome for degradation, and 
consequently decreases their protein levels in small intestine and interferes with nutrient 
absorption (11). It has also been reported that ubiquitination of CD36 serves as a sorting 
signaling for its lysosomal degradation after internalized into early/sorting endosomes (34). 
One possibility is that this ubiquitination-dependent pathway for lysosomal degradation of 
CD36 might be chronically activated in Rab8a-deficient skeletal muscle, which might 
decrease CD36 proteins in older mice. This chronic CD36-degradation signal might be absent 
in the acute Rab8a-knockdown culture cell system due to either its possible time-dependent 
nature or potential non-cell-autonomous origin. 
LDs are important organelles for lipid storage in many tissues including skeletal 
muscle and adipose tissues (7). Despite LDs in these two tissues having different sizes, our 
studies demonstrate that LD fusion requires Rab8a as a common regulator in both skeletal 
muscle and adipose tissues (this study and (17)). Our data also show that lipid storage 
through LD fusion might be coordinated with lipid uptake in skeletal muscle, and Rab8a was 
involved in both processes. Fatty acids and their derivatives can cause lipotoxicity to skeletal 
muscle, and their conversion into triglycerides can facilitate detoxification of fatty acids (6). 
We suspect that the possible coordination between lipid uptake and storage via Rab8a might 
help to reduce lipotoxicity in skeletal muscle.

Our study demonstrates the importance of skeletal muscle in regulation of 
whole-body lipid homeostasis through communicating with lipogenic and cholesterol 
biosynthetic pathways in the liver. The interaction between muscle and liver storage of lipid 
is not a simple process of substrate redistribution from the muscle into the liver. Rather, it is a 
cross-talk between these two organs involving induction of lipogenic and cholesterol 
biosynthetic genes in the liver through the mTOR-lipin1-SREBP1 pathway. Although our 
data suggest serum lipids as important mediators in regulation of hepatic mTOR activation in 
the Rab8a-mKO mice, it is possible that some other skeletal muscle-derived factors might 
also contribute to this activation. Physical inactivity is one of the underlying causes of 
NAFLD (35), and exercise is an effective treatment to combat NAFLD and can lower liver 
fat in the absence of significant weight loss (36; 37). The mechanisms by which exercise 
decreases liver fat are not fully understood although it is conceivable that multiple pathways 
may be involved. Interestingly, exercise can elevate the lipid content of skeletal muscle (38). 
It is therefore an intriguing question whether the organ cross-talk between skeletal muscle 
and liver identified in this study may contribute to the therapeutic effects of exercise on 
NAFLD, which is deserving of further investigation in future. 
In summary, our findings demonstrate that Rab8a is an important molecule regulating 
both lipid uptake and LD fusion in skeletal muscle. Lipid entry into skeletal muscle for 
subsequent metabolism or storage is important for whole-body lipid homeostasis, and its 
impairment causes hyperlipidemia and promotes NAFLD.
